title: NCAA proposes penalties to deter teams from circumventing transfer portal in the spring
content:
The NCAA took a significant step in its effort to deter teams from circumventing the transfer portal by proposing major penalties — including head coach suspensions — for schools that add non-portal players this spring and beyond.

The NCAA’s Division I FBS oversight committee on Wednesday recommended that if FBS schools add a transfer who is not already in the transfer portal and did not enter during a designated window, the head coach of that school would be suspended for six games — half of the regular season. That suspension would include a prohibition on all football activities (recruiting and on-field coaching) and administrative duties (team meetings).

In addition to the head coach suspension, schools that violate the rule would also be fined 20 percent of their football budget and lose five roster spots for the next season, regardless of whether the head coach in charge during the time of the violation is still employed at the school.

The proposal still requires approval and will be on the docket at the Division I cabinet’s April meeting. If passed, it would become effective immediately.

“We felt this was appropriate to place an emphasis on this rule with where we are in Division I football,” said Mark Alnutt, chair of the oversight committee and director of athletics at Buffalo, in a statement. “We have a window for student-athletes to notify their school when they would like to enter the transfer portal. If there is movement without going through the process as it is legislated, the committee felt there needed to be significant penalties.”

College football’s transfer portal windows began during the 2022-23 offseason as a way to deter players from entering the portal during the playing season. There were two portal windows — one in winter and one in spring — until this offseason, when the sport moved to one window, which opened on Jan. 2 and closed on Jan. 16.

What teams and players would do without a spring portal window has been a topic of interest in the sport since the January portal window closed. Multiple general managers and personnel directors who have spoken with The Athletic this offseason suspected that, following spring football when depth charts were set and coaches had a better feel for their squads, players might simply unenroll from one school and enroll at another — like a traditional student would — without using the portal.

That transfer method, which was utilized last offseason by defensive back Xavier Lucas (who transferred from Wisconsin to Miami) and quarterback Jake Retzlaff (BYU to Tulane), has been permissible. The caveat is that schools are prohibited from making recruiting contact with players unless they are in the portal. But coaches and personnel staffers acknowledge that the NCAA’s policing of tampering has been largely fruitless.

The FBS oversight committee’s proposal would theoretically close the unenroll/enroll loophole.

Recently, a Power 4 general manager, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the topic, proposed suspending coaches as a solution to tampering and told The Athletic that if coaches were suspended for multiple games, “I guarantee you (tampering) would slow down.”

Although the NCAA’s proposal limits suspensions to head coaches, the length of the suspension, reduction in football budget and loss of roster spots would likely be a strong deterrent.

Budgets are already strained across the country as schools have begun to pay players directly with the institution of revenue sharing, a result of the House v. NCAA settlement that was approved last year.

Part of that settlement also included a cap on roster spots instead of scholarships. Football programs are currently limited to 105 roster spots. So a team that is proven to violate this new rule, if approved, would be limited to 100 players on its roster the following season.

This proposal focuses only on teams that add players outside the portal window and does not apply to tampering in the traditional sense, where teams try to entice players at other schools to enter the portal during the designated window. That remains a rampant issue that the sport’s power brokers have decried. GMs and personnel directors have said that tampering was widespread in December, as teams worked with player agents to get ahead of the curve before the portal opened on Jan. 2.

But what this rule will do, if passed, is basically eliminate an unofficial spring portal window. When teams have needs or players become disenchanted with where they are on the depth chart following spring football practice, it won’t be as easy as just leaving their school and showing up at another. The stiff nature of the penalties should keep teams from risking such a move.

Chances are, if teams have needs following spring practice, they may look into players who are still in the portal but haven’t signed anywhere. Division II, which doesn’t have a specific portal window, could be an outlet, as could the junior college ranks, which used to be heavily utilized by schools for transfers before the portal was instituted in 2018.

College football’s current portal window lasts for 15 days in January, but there are a few exceptions. Players on teams who have a head coaching change get a 15-day portal window that begins five days after a new coach is hired. If a new coach is not hired within 30 days, the 15-day window begins on the 31st day after the coaching change.

Players on College Football Playoff teams whose seasons extend beyond the closing of the portal window get a five-day window to enter the portal. That period begins the day after their final game of the season.
